name: OpenSpec
description: Spec-driven development (SDD) for AI coding assistants.
readmeExcerpt:
The most loved spec framework.

Our philosophy: ```text → fluid not rigid → iterative not waterfall → easy not complex → built for brownfield not just greenfield → scalable from personal projects to enterprises ```

Follow @0xTab on X for updates · Join the OpenSpec Discord for help and questions.

## See it in action ```text You: /openspec-explore AI: What would you like to explore? You: I want dark mode but I'm not sure how to do it cleanly. AI: Let me look at your styling setup... Cleanest path here: CSS variables + a small theme context, with system-preference detection. No new dependencies. Scope it? You: Yes, let's do it. You: /openspec-propose add-dark-mode AI: Created openspec/changes/add-dark-mode/ ✓ proposal.md — why we're doing this, what's changing ✓ specs/ — requirements and scenarios ✓ design.md — technical approach ✓ tasks.md — implementation checklist Ready for implementation! You: /openspec-apply-change AI: Implementing tasks... ✓ 1.1 Add theme context provider ✓ 1.2 Create toggle component ✓ 2.1 Add CSS variables ✓ 2.2 Wire up localStorage All tasks complete! You: /openspec-archive-change AI: Archived to openspec/changes/archive/2025-01-23-add-dark-mode/ Specs updated. Ready for the next feature. ```
What do the specs actually look like? Plain Markdown — requirements with concrete scenarios, no special syntax to learn. Here's what goes in the `specs/` folder created above: ```markdown ## ADDED Requirements ### Requirement: Theme selection The app SHALL let users switch between light and dark themes, defaulting to the system preference. #### Scenario: User toggles dark mode - **WHEN** the user clicks the theme toggle - **THEN** the app switches to dark mode and persists the choice ``` Your AI writes these; you review the plan before any code is written. OpenSpec is built with OpenSpec — browse this repo's live [specs](openspec/specs) and in-flight [changes](openspec/changes) for real examples at scale.
OpenSpec Dashboard

## Why teams adopt OpenSpec Solo, OpenSpec keeps you and your AI honest on a single repo. On a team, the hard part moves: a feature spans the API server, the web app, and a shared library; requirements are owned by one team and consumed by others; planning starts before any code exists. **[Stores](https://openspec.dev/docs/stores)** are the answer — planning in a repo of its own. The same `openspec/` shape you already know (specs and changes), shared by `git push` like anything else. One source of truth your whole team and every coding agent can read, across every repo. - **Cross-repo features** — one change, one plan, even when the code lands in three repos. - **Shared requirements** — a platform team owns the specs; product teams reference them read-only, right where their coding agent can read them. No drifting wiki. - **Plan before code** — capture the plan in the store now; the code repos catch up later. > Stores are in **beta**. Start with the [Stores guide](https://openspec.dev/docs/stores). ## Quick Start Install OpenSpec. On macOS or Linux, in your terminal: ```bash curl -fsSL https://openspec.dev/cli/install.sh | sh ``` On Windows, in PowerShell: ```powershell irm https://openspec.dev/cli/install.ps1 | iex ``` Prefer a package manager? `npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest` (needs Node.js 22.20.0 or higher) or the official [Homebrew formula](https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/openspec), `brew install openspec`. Then navigate to your project directory and initialize: ```bash cd your-project openspec init ``` > **Want your AI to do it?** Paste the [setup prompt](https://openspec.dev/docs/installation#install-with-your-ai-assistant) into your coding assistant — it installs the CLI, runs `openspec init`, and verifies the result. Now talk to your AI: - **Not sure what to build yet?** Start with `/openspec-explore`, a no-stakes thinking partner that reads your code, weighs options, and shapes a plan before any code gets written. ([Quickstart](https://openspec.dev/docs/quickstart)) - **Already know what you want?** Go straight to `/openspec-propose `. Both are in the default profile. If you want the expanded workflow (`openspec-new-change`, `openspec-continue-change`, `openspec-ff-change`, `openspec-verify-change`, `openspec-bulk-archive-change`, `openspec-onboard`), select it with `openspec config profile` and apply with `openspec update`. These are skills. Most tools invoke them as `/openspec-propose` and Codex as `$openspec-propose`, or you can ask for the work in plain words. `openspec init` prints the right form for the tools you picked — see [Supported Tools](https://openspec.dev/docs/supported-tools). Coming from 1.x and its `/opsx:*` commands? See [Upgrade to 2.0](https://openspec.dev/docs/upgrade-to-2). > [!NOTE] > Not sure if your tool is supported? [View the full list](https://openspec.dev/docs/supported-tools) – we support 30+ tools and growing. > > Also works with npm, Homebrew, pnpm, yarn, bun, and Nix. [See installation options](https://openspec.dev/docs/installation). ## Docs Full documentation lives at **[openspec.dev/docs](https://openspec.dev/docs)**. → **[Quickstart](https://openspec.dev/docs/quickstart)**: your first change, start to finish
→ **[Set up your project](https://openspec.dev/docs/setup)**: what `openspec init` installs
→ **[CLI](https://openspec.dev/docs/cli)**: terminal reference
→ **[Supported Tools](https://openspec.dev/docs/supported-tools)**: tool integrations & install paths
→ **[Customize](https://openspec.dev/docs/customize)**: profiles, project config, and schemas
→ **[Stores](https://openspec.dev/docs/stores)**: plan in a separate repo, shared across your team (beta)
→ **[Community Showcase](docs/community.md)**: projects and resources built with and for OpenSpec ## Community schemas Third-party schema bundles distributed via standalone repositories — these provide opinionated workflows that integrate OpenSpec with other tools, similar to how [github/spec-kit's community extension catalog](https://github.com/github/spec-kit/tree/main/extensions) handles tool integrations. → **[Browse the catalog](docs/customization.md#community-schemas)** in the customization docs. ## Why OpenSpec? AI coding assistants are powerful but unpredictable when requirements live only in chat history. OpenSpec adds a lightweight spec layer so you agree on what to build before any code is written. - **Agree before you build** — human and AI align on specs before code gets written - **Stay organized** — each change gets its own folder with proposal, specs, design, and tasks - **Work fluidly** — update any artifact anytime, no rigid phase gates - **Use your tools** — works with 30+ AI assistants via skills ### How we compare **vs. [Spec Kit](https://github.com/github/spec-kit)** (GitHub) — Thorough but heavyweight. Rigid phase gates, lots of Markdown, Python setup. OpenSpec is lighter and lets you iterate freely. **vs. [Kiro](https://kiro.dev)** (AWS) — Powerful but you're locked into their IDE and limited to Claude models. OpenSpec works with the tools you already use. **vs. nothing** — AI coding without specs means vague prompts and unpredictable results. OpenSpec brings predictability without the ceremony. ## Updating OpenSpec **Upgrade the CLI** With the standalone install, run `openspec install`. If you installed with npm: ```bash npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest ``` If you installed OpenSpec with Homebrew: ```bash brew upgrade openspec ``` **Refresh agent instructions** Run this once to refresh the skills installed on your machine. If your team keeps skills in Git, run it in each project that commits them. ```bash openspec update ``` ## Usage Notes **Model selection**: OpenSpec works best with high-reasoning models. We recommend Codex 5.5 and Opus 4.7 for both planning and implementation. **Context hygiene**: OpenSpec benefits from a clean context window. Clear your context before starting implementation and maintain good context hygiene throughout your session. ## Contributing Every change starts as an issue. We discuss it there, and if we agree to pursue it, a maintainer implements the change or invites you to build it with us. → **[CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md)**: the full process, from first issue to merged PR ## Other
Telemetry OpenSpec collects anonymous usage stats. We collect only command names and version to understand usage patterns. No arguments, paths, content, or PII. Automatically disabled in CI. **Opt-out (any one is enough):** - `openspec config set telemetry.enabled false` (global config; unset means on) - `export OPENSPEC_TELEMETRY=0` or `export DO_NOT_TRACK=1` (env overrides config)
Maintainers & Advisors See [MAINTAINERS.md](MAINTAINERS.md) for the list of core maintainers and advisors who help guide the project.

releases.name: v2.1.1 - Offline skill installs, safer archive
releases.body:
# OpenSpec 2.1.1

This release smooths out a handful of rough edges. Skills now install straight from the CLI, with no Git and no network needed. Archive is more careful with your main specs, and `validate --strict` catches two problems before they reach archive. Your workflows don't change.

## How to upgrade

Update the OpenSpec CLI, then run this in each project:

```bash
openspec update
```

## Skills install from the CLI itself

- **No more Git or GitHub needed to install skills.** In 2.1.0, `openspec init` and `openspec update` cloned the skills from GitHub, so they failed without Git, behind a strict firewall, or offline. The skills now come from the CLI package you already installed, so setup works anywhere and the skills always match your CLI version.
- **`npx skills add` installs stay up to date.** If you added the OpenSpec skills to a project with `npx skills add`, `openspec update` used to skip them. It now finds them and refreshes them like any other install.
- **The continue workflow hands off to apply again.** When planning is complete, the continue skill tells you the plan is ready to review and that you can ask your agent to apply it.

releases.name: v2.1.0 - Global skills
releases.body:
# OpenSpec 2.1

OpenSpec now supports global skills for coding agents. Install the skills once and your agent can use them in every project on your machine.

As more teams adopt Vercel’s `skills` installer, it’s becoming a common way to install skills across coding tools. OpenSpec is adopting it too, so we can spend less time maintaining installer code and more time improving the skills themselves.

The OpenSpec workflows themselves haven't changed.

## What changed

- **Skills can be installed globally.** Vercel’s installer handles the location for each supported agent, whether it reads `~/.agents/skills/` or uses its own folder.
- **`openspec update` asks where a project's skills should live.** In a repo that has its own OpenSpec skills, you choose once between keeping them in the repo and switching to global. Nothing changes until you choose.
- **`openspec init --tools <ids>` in a new repo installs globally.** In 2.0 it wrote the skills into the repo. Add `--scope project` to keep them there.
- **Skills are installed by Vercel’s `skills` package.** Installing or refreshing them needs Git and access to GitHub.

## How to upgrade

Update the OpenSpec CLI, then run this in each pro

releases.name: v2.0.0 - Skills in .agents/skills, /opsx commands removed
releases.body:
# OpenSpec 2.0

OpenSpec now installs skills in `.agents/skills/` instead of keeping a separate copy for each coding agent. Tools that don't read this folder, like Claude Code and Kiro, get links to the same skills.

We're also removing the `/opsx:*` slash commands. Each command already has a matching skill, so there's no need to maintain both.

The OpenSpec workflows themselves haven't changed.

## What changed

- **Skills are installed in `.agents/skills/`.** Every tool uses the same skills, without duplicate files across folders.
- **`/opsx:*` commands are removed.** For example, `/opsx:propose` becomes `/openspec-propose` (or `$openspec-propose` in Codex). You can also just ask your agent for the work.
- **`openspec update` removes files generated by older versions.** This includes old slash commands and duplicate skills. Files you've changed in the old locations are kept and listed.
- The `delivery` setting is no longer needed. Existing configs keep working.
- Amazon Q Developer support is removed because it can't load skills. We recommend Kiro instead.

## How to upgrade

Update the OpenSpec CLI, then run this in each project and commit the changes:

```bash
openspec update
`

releases.name: v1.17.0 - Safe upgrades, 2.0 notice
releases.body:
## What's New in v1.17.0

`openspec update` now upgrades a project from any older release in one run, and announces that command files go away in OpenSpec 2.0.

> **Heads-up: command files (`/opsx:*`) go away in OpenSpec 2.0.** Your OpenSpec skills stay and do the same work. To switch now, run `openspec config set delivery skills && openspec update`. The plan is in [#2022](https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec/issues/2022).

### New

- **2.0 notice** - While a configured tool still gets command files, `openspec update` ends with a short notice that they go away in 2.0, plus the one command to switch early. It stays silent once you use skills only, and for tools without command files, such as Codex.

### Improved

- **Upgrades from any release** - `openspec update` now upgrades a project made by any release since 0.12 in one run, without stopping to ask for `--force`. It removes old OpenSpec files nobody edited, including leftover copies that made some tools show every skill twice, and keeps any file you changed.
- **Safer cleanup** - Cleanup never touches files outside your project, even when a folder inside it links somewhere else, and never removes anything when a tool fails to

releases.name: v1.16.1 - Spec parsing, version checks
releases.body:
## What's New in v1.16.1

A patch release that makes spec validation stricter and more forgiving in the right places, and makes `openspec version --check` reliable.

### Fixed

- **Closed section headings** - `validate`, `show`, `list`, `view` and `archive` now read headings with a closing `#` run (`## Purpose ##`, `## ADDED Requirements ##`) the same as their unclosed forms.
- **Unrecognized delta sections** - `validate` now fails, and `archive` refuses, when a delta spec puts a requirement under an unrecognized section such as `## DEPRECATED Requirements`, instead of passing with a warning and silently dropping that requirement.
- **Version check with telemetry off** - `openspec version --check` now checks for a newer version even when telemetry is off or it runs in CI. Only `OPENSPEC_NO_UPDATE_CHECK` skips it; the background check in `openspec update` still honors the telemetry opt-out and CI.
- **Standalone update offers** - `openspec version --check` on the standalone binary now offers only a release whose files are attached on GitHub, the same one `openspec install` would install, rather than a version npm has before the installer can get it.

The most loved spec framework.

Our philosophy: 
→ fluid not rigid
→ iterative not waterfall
→ easy not complex
→ built for brownfield not just greenfield
→ scalable from personal projects to enterprises

Follow @0xTab on X for updates · Join the OpenSpec Discord for help and questions.

See it in action

You: /openspec-explore
AI:  What would you like to explore?
You: I want dark mode but I'm not sure how to do it cleanly.
AI:  Let me look at your styling setup...
     Cleanest path here: CSS variables + a small theme context,
     with system-preference detection. No new dependencies. Scope it?
You: Yes, let's do it.

You: /openspec-propose add-dark-mode
AI:  Created openspec/changes/add-dark-mode/
     ✓ proposal.md — why we're doing this, what's changing
     ✓ specs/       — requirements and scenarios
     ✓ design.md    — technical approach
     ✓ tasks.md     — implementation checklist
     Ready for implementation!

You: /openspec-apply-change
AI:  Implementing tasks...
     ✓ 1.1 Add theme context provider
     ✓ 1.2 Create toggle component
     ✓ 2.1 Add CSS variables
     ✓ 2.2 Wire up localStorage
     All tasks complete!

You: /openspec-archive-change
AI:  Archived to openspec/changes/archive/2025-01-23-add-dark-mode/
     Specs updated. Ready for the next feature.
What do the specs actually look like?

Plain Markdown — requirements with concrete scenarios, no special syntax to learn. Here's what goes in the specs/ folder created above:

## ADDED Requirements

### Requirement: Theme selection
The app SHALL let users switch between light and dark themes,
defaulting to the system preference.

#### Scenario: User toggles dark mode
- **WHEN** the user clicks the theme toggle
- **THEN** the app switches to dark mode and persists the choice

Your AI writes these; you review the plan before any code is written.

OpenSpec is built with OpenSpec — browse this repo's live specs and in-flight changes for real examples at scale.

OpenSpec Dashboard

Why teams adopt OpenSpec

Solo, OpenSpec keeps you and your AI honest on a single repo. On a team, the hard part moves: a feature spans the API server, the web app, and a shared library; requirements are owned by one team and consumed by others; planning starts before any code exists.

Stores are the answer — planning in a repo of its own. The same openspec/ shape you already know (specs and changes), shared by git push like anything else. One source of truth your whole team and every coding agent can read, across every repo.

  • Cross-repo features — one change, one plan, even when the code lands in three repos.
  • Shared requirements — a platform team owns the specs; product teams reference them read-only, right where their coding agent can read them. No drifting wiki.
  • Plan before code — capture the plan in the store now; the code repos catch up later.

Stores are in beta. Start with the Stores guide.

Quick Start

Install OpenSpec. On macOS or Linux, in your terminal:

curl -fsSL https://openspec.dev/cli/install.sh | sh

On Windows, in PowerShell:

irm https://openspec.dev/cli/install.ps1 | iex

Prefer a package manager? npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest (needs Node.js 22.20.0 or higher) or the official Homebrew formula, brew install openspec.

Then navigate to your project directory and initialize:

cd your-project
openspec init

Want your AI to do it? Paste the setup prompt into your coding assistant — it installs the CLI, runs openspec init, and verifies the result.

Now talk to your AI:

  • Not sure what to build yet? Start with /openspec-explore, a no-stakes thinking partner that reads your code, weighs options, and shapes a plan before any code gets written. (Quickstart)
  • Already know what you want? Go straight to /openspec-propose <what-you-want-to-build>.

Both are in the default profile. If you want the expanded workflow (openspec-new-change, openspec-continue-change, openspec-ff-change, openspec-verify-change, openspec-bulk-archive-change, openspec-onboard), select it with openspec config profile and apply with openspec update.

These are skills. Most tools invoke them as /openspec-propose and Codex as $openspec-propose, or you can ask for the work in plain words. openspec init prints the right form for the tools you picked — see Supported Tools. Coming from 1.x and its /opsx:* commands? See Upgrade to 2.0.

Note

Not sure if your tool is supported? View the full list – we support 30+ tools and growing.

Also works with npm, Homebrew, pnpm, yarn, bun, and Nix. See installation options.

Docs

Full documentation lives at openspec.dev/docs.

→ Quickstart: your first change, start to finish
→ Set up your project: what openspec init installs
→ CLI: terminal reference
→ Supported Tools: tool integrations & install paths
→ Customize: profiles, project config, and schemas
→ Stores: plan in a separate repo, shared across your team (beta)
→ Community Showcase: projects and resources built with and for OpenSpec

Community schemas

Third-party schema bundles distributed via standalone repositories — these provide opinionated workflows that integrate OpenSpec with other tools, similar to how github/spec-kit's community extension catalog handles tool integrations.

→ Browse the catalog in the customization docs.

Why OpenSpec?

AI coding assistants are powerful but unpredictable when requirements live only in chat history. OpenSpec adds a lightweight spec layer so you agree on what to build before any code is written.

  • Agree before you build — human and AI align on specs before code gets written
  • Stay organized — each change gets its own folder with proposal, specs, design, and tasks
  • Work fluidly — update any artifact anytime, no rigid phase gates
  • Use your tools — works with 30+ AI assistants via skills

How we compare

vs. Spec Kit (GitHub) — Thorough but heavyweight. Rigid phase gates, lots of Markdown, Python setup. OpenSpec is lighter and lets you iterate freely.

vs. Kiro (AWS) — Powerful but you're locked into their IDE and limited to Claude models. OpenSpec works with the tools you already use.

vs. nothing — AI coding without specs means vague prompts and unpredictable results. OpenSpec brings predictability without the ceremony.

Updating OpenSpec

Upgrade the CLI

With the standalone install, run openspec install. If you installed with npm:

npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest

If you installed OpenSpec with Homebrew:

brew upgrade openspec

Refresh agent instructions

Run this once to refresh the skills installed on your machine. If your team keeps skills in Git, run it in each project that commits them.

openspec update

Usage Notes

Model selection: OpenSpec works best with high-reasoning models. We recommend Codex 5.5 and Opus 4.7 for both planning and implementation.

Context hygiene: OpenSpec benefits from a clean context window. Clear your context before starting implementation and maintain good context hygiene throughout your session.

Contributing

Every change starts as an issue. We discuss it there, and if we agree to pursue it, a maintainer implements the change or invites you to build it with us.

→ CONTRIBUTING.md: the full process, from first issue to merged PR

Other

Telemetry

OpenSpec collects anonymous usage stats.

We collect only command names and version to understand usage patterns. No arguments, paths, content, or PII. Automatically disabled in CI.

Opt-out (any one is enough):

  • openspec config set telemetry.enabled false (global config; unset means on)
  • export OPENSPEC_TELEMETRY=0 or export DO_NOT_TRACK=1 (env overrides config)
Maintainers & Advisors

See MAINTAINERS.md for the list of core maintainers and advisors who help guide the project.

License

MIT

aiSummary.oneLiner: A spec-driven development framework promoting fluid and iterative software specifications for AI coding assistants.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: OpenSpec introduces an iterative spec-driven development methodology tailored for modern AI coding assistants. The framework replaces rigid waterfall planning with an artifact-guided workflow that remains fluid and easily adaptable throughout the software development lifecycle. By utilizing context engineering, the tool enables AI agents to better understand and act upon software design documents and product requirements. This approach scales seamlessly from small personal tools to large enterprise architectures, specifically accommodating brownfield projects rather than just greenfield deployments.
keyFeatures: Iterative specification: Promotes fluid and adaptable software design documents rather than rigid waterfall planning.
AI assistant integration: Tailors product requirements and system architecture documents specifically for AI agents to process.
Artifact-guided workflow: Uses structured artifacts to direct the software development lifecycle effectively.
Brownfield support: Adapts seamlessly to existing legacy codebases rather than solely focusing on new greenfield projects.
Scalable architecture: Handles varying project complexities from individual developer tools to comprehensive enterprise systems.

useCases.description: Maintain fluid product requirements that can evolve dynamically as project assumptions change.

useCases.description: Generate clear architectural specifications for existing legacy systems to assist new developers or AI tools.
